system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2149-10-31 20:45:00 to 2149-11-01 14:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for recurrent abdominal pain similar to prior pancreatitis episodes, but with normal lipase levels and only mild CT findings. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and pain control, then gradually advanced to a solid diet. A UTI was treated with a 3-day course of levofloxacin. EGD and capsule endoscopy revealed chronic duodenitis, suggesting possible small bowel disease or IBD, though the etiology remained unclear. A colonoscopy was attempted but unsuccessful due to inadequate bowel prep, requiring a future repeat with full GoLytely preparation. Her orthostatic hypotension was managed with dose adjustments to fludrocortisone and betaxolol, and she was discharged home in good condition, tolerating oral intake and requiring no IV medications.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Known cystic lesion of the pancreas and prior episodes of
pancreatitis, please evaluate for flow through the main pancreatic duct.

COMPARISON:  MRCP of ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired through the
abdomen on a 1.5 Tesla magnet, including dynamic high-resolution 3D imaging
obtained prior to, during, and after the uneventful intravenous administration
of 0.1 mmol/kg (15 mL) of gadolinium-DTPA.  Thick-slab SSFSE images were
obtained through the pancreatic duct prior to and following the intravenous
administration of 13.5 mcg of secretin at 30 second intervals for 10 minutes.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformatted and subtraction images were generated and
reviewed on a separate workstation.

FINDINGS:  Again seen in the tail of the pancreas are two small cystic
lesions, measuring 8 x 8 mm (100:55, 8:20) and 4-mm (8:19; 100:60), both of
which display homogeneous T2 hyperintensity and lack enhancement after the
administration of gadolinium and which are unchanged in size.  The pancreatic
duct is nondilated.  Following the administration of secretin, there is
transient dilation of the duct with prompt return to pre-secretin caliber, and
marked secretion of fluid into the duodenum with prompt transit beyond the
ligament of Treitz.  The pancreatic parenchyma enhances homogeneously without
evidence of solid enhancing masses.

The mild irregularity of the intrahepatic bile ducts which was noted on the
previous study is less apparent on today's study, and several foci of patchy
T2 hyperintensity previously present in the hepatic parenchyma are no longer
visualized.  No enhancing hepatic masses are identified.  The portal vein is
patent.  The gallbladder is nondistended.

The spleen and adrenal glands appear unremarkable.  No renal masses or
hydronephrosis are present.  There are no pathologically enlarged mesenteric
or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.  The imaged loops of small bowel appear within
normal limits.

The abdominal aorta is normal in caliber.  Although mild irregularity of the
celiac axis is again noted, this finding may be artifactual and appears
unchanged.

The imaged marrow signal appears within normal limits.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations and subtraction images were essential in
delineating the above-described findings.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No interval change in two cystic lesions of the pancreatic tail up to 8 mm
in diameter.
2.  Normal secretin examination of the pancreas.
3.  Previously noted irregularity of the biliary ducts is no longer apparent
on today's examination, although attention on further followup imaging is
recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain since your test today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started during the MRCP when they gave me that secretin shot. It was sharp, right here in the upper belly, but only lasted a few minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And then it came back later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About two hours after I got home. It got worse—radiated to my back, with nausea. I took my usual Dilaudid, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a flare of pancreatitis, especially given your history. We’ll keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? But the pain was only brief during the test. Is this really pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, secretin can trigger it, even if the test itself is safe for most. Your symptoms are classic—epigastric pain, nausea, radiation to the back. We’ve started IV fluids and will give you IV pain meds to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My lipase was only 40 in the ER—is that high enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s on the lower side, but we don’t always see big enzyme rises, especially with mild or early episodes. Your history and symptoms guide us more here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The IV meds helped. I’m not nauseous anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow if you stay comfortable. We also reviewed your MRCP—no changes in the cysts, and your pancreatic duct responded normally to secretin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are the cysts still there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but they’re small and unchanged—8 mm and under, no signs of concern. The biliary irregularities we saw before are also less noticeable, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. You’re pain-free and tolerating sips. We’ll advance you to a soft diet and get ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds? I take Creon, omeprazole, and the ones for my blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all of them. We’re adjusting your fludrocortisone to half dose—0.1 mg twice daily—because you tend to get low potassium. Midodrine you’ll restart at home when you’re up and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my antidepressant and amitriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. We lowered amitriptyline to 25 mg at night to help with side effects, but it’s still important for sleep and nerve-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable, and you’ve eaten without pain. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid fatty and high-protein foods for a few days. Reintroduce them slowly. If you develop fever, chills, or vomiting, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule a visit with your gastroenterologist to review the MRCP and your pancreatitis history. Keep taking Creon with all meals—six capsules now, as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You responded well. Just take it easy the next few days, stay hydrated, and follow the diet plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll follow up as scheduled.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with acute pancreatitis triggered by secretin administration during an MRCP, presenting with epigastric pain radiating to the back and nausea. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and IV pain control, then gradually advanced to a soft diet as symptoms resolved. Her pancreatic cysts remained stable on imaging, and biliary irregularities improved. Fludrocortisone was adjusted to 0.1 mg BID to prevent hypokalemia, and midodrine was held during admission per patient preference. She was discharged home in good condition, tolerating oral intake, with instructions to avoid fatty foods and monitor for fever or vomiting.
